stem: Arrange the following Indian statutes in the chronological order of their enactment:
items: Copyright Act
Information Technology Act
Patents Act
Trade Marks Act
explanation: Copyright Act 1957, Patents Act 1970, Trade Marks Act 1999 and Information Technology Act 2000.

stem: Match List I (crossing of a cheque) with List II (effect):
listII: The name of a particular banker is added across the cheque
The holder cannot get a better title than that of the transferor
Two parallel transverse lines, with or without words such as '& Co.'
Proceeds are to be credited only to the payee's account
explanation: A general crossing uses two parallel lines, a special crossing names a banker, 'not negotiable' removes the possibility of a better title, and 'account payee' directs the collecting banker to credit only the payee.

stem: Consider the following statements with reference to the Consumer Protection Act, 2019:
items: A person who buys goods through electronic means is covered by the definition of consumer.
A person who obtains goods for resale or for a commercial purpose is generally not a consumer.
A product liability action may be brought against a product manufacturer, a product service provider or a product seller.
A complaint can be filed only where the opposite party resides or carries on business.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The 2019 Act also allows a complaint to be filed where the complainant resides or personally works for gain.

stem: Consider the following statements about agency under the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
items: A principal is not bound by the acts of the agent done within the scope of the agent's authority.
Any person who is of the age of majority and of sound mind may employ an agent.
No consideration is necessary to create an agency.
An agency may be created by ratification of acts done without authority.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 2, 3 and 4 are correct. A principal is bound by acts of the agent done within the scope of his authority.

stem: Under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a cheque is a bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker and:
options: Not expressed to be payable otherwise than on demand
Payable on a fixed future date
Payable only after acceptance by the drawee
explanation: Section 6 defines a cheque as a bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker and not expressed to be payable otherwise than on demand.

stem: Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise is called:
explanation: Section 172 defines pledge as bailment of goods as security; hypothecation involves no transfer of possession, and a mortgage relates to immovable property.

stem: Consider the following statements about the minimum number of directors under the Companies Act, 2013:
items: A private company must have at least two directors.
A public company must have at least three directors.
At least one-third of the total directors of a listed public company must be independent directors.
A One Person Company must have at least two directors.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. A One Person Company needs a minimum of only one director.

stem: Match List I (form of business organisation) with List II (feature):
listII: Separate legal entity managed by a board of directors on behalf of shareholders
Single owner with unlimited liability
Separate legal entity with limited liability and internal structure fixed by agreement
No separate legal entity; partners have unlimited liability
explanation: An LLP combines corporate personality and limited liability with partnership-style flexibility; a general partnership has unlimited liability; a company is run by a board for its shareholders; a sole proprietor owns the business alone.

stem: Under the Companies Act, 2013, a One Person Company is formed as a:
explanation: The Act introduced the One Person Company as a type of private company having only one member.

stem: Contraventions under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 are treated as:
explanation: Unlike FERA, FEMA treats contraventions as civil in nature, attracting monetary penalties, and allows them to be compounded.

stem: Under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the person who makes a promissory note is called the:
explanation: A promissory note has two parties: the maker, who promises to pay, and the payee; drawer and drawee are parties to a bill of exchange or cheque.

stem: Consider the following statements about LLPs under the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008:
items: The provisions of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 do not apply to an LLP.
A private company may convert into an LLP in accordance with the Act.
An LLP must have a minimum paid-up capital of ₹1 lakh.
An obligation of the LLP, whether arising in contract or otherwise, is solely the obligation of the LLP.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. The Act prescribes no minimum capital for an LLP; partners' contribution is decided by the LLP agreement.

stem: Consider the following statements with reference to the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
items: An agreement in restraint of the marriage of any person other than a minor is void.
An agreement by way of wager is void.
Every agreement in restraint of trade is void without any exception.
A contract whose consent is caused by coercion is voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Agreements in restraint of trade are void, but the Act saves an agreement by the seller of goodwill not to carry on a similar business within specified local limits.

stem: Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, arrange the following events of a contract made by post in chronological order:
items: The acceptance comes to the knowledge of the proposer
The proposer posts the letter of proposal
The proposal comes to the knowledge of the offeree
The offeree posts the letter of acceptance
explanation: Communication of a proposal is complete when it reaches the offeree; acceptance is complete against the proposer when posted, and against the acceptor when it reaches the proposer (Section 4).

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Competition Act, 2002, merely holding a dominant position is not prohibited.
reason: Reason (R): The Competition Commission of India is a body corporate having perpetual succession and a common seal.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both are true, but A holds because the Act prohibits only the abuse of a dominant position; the corporate status of the CCI does not explain it.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, consideration must move from the promisee only.
reason: Reason (R): Under the Act, consideration may move from the promisee or from any other person, at the desire of the promisor.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Section 2(d) allows consideration to move from the promisee or any other person, so A is false and R is true (see also Chinnaya v. Ramayya).

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless otherwise provided by the contract.
reason: Reason (R): Under the Act, a contract of guarantee may be either oral or written.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both are true (Sections 128 and 126), but the form in which a guarantee may be made has nothing to do with the extent of the surety's liability.

stem: Arrange the following Indian statutes in the chronological order of their enactment:
items: Indian Partnership Act
Sale of Goods Act
Indian Contract Act
Negotiable Instruments Act
explanation: Indian Contract Act 1872, Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, Sale of Goods Act 1930 and Indian Partnership Act 1932.

stem: Consider the following statements with reference to the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999:
items: One of its objectives is to facilitate external trade and payments.
The Directorate of Enforcement investigates contraventions under the Act.
Residential status under the Act is determined exactly as under the income-tax law.
The Act also applies to branches, offices and agencies outside India owned or controlled by a person resident in India.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. FEMA has its own definition of 'person resident in India' (based on stay of more than 182 days in the preceding financial year plus intention), which differs from income-tax rules.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, an unpaid seller loses his right of lien when the buyer lawfully obtains possession of the goods.
reason: Reason (R): Lien is a right to retain possession of goods until the price is paid or tendered.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Because lien is a possessory right, it cannot survive once the goods have lawfully passed into the buyer's possession; R therefore explains A.

stem: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the authority established to regulate violations of consumer rights, unfair trade practices and false or misleading advertisements is the:
explanation: The 2019 Act created the Central Consumer Protection Authority as a regulator; the Commissions adjudicate disputes and the Councils are advisory bodies.

stem: Match List I (type of company under the Companies Act, 2013) with List II (feature):
listII: Private company with paid-up capital and turnover below prescribed limits
Has only one person as a member
Promotes charitable objects and prohibits payment of dividend to members
Not less than 51% of paid-up share capital held by government
explanation: An OPC has one member, a Section 8 company applies income to its charitable objects without paying dividends, a government company has at least 51% government shareholding, and a small company is defined by capital and turnover thresholds.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Copyright Act, 1957, copyright protects ideas as such.
reason: Reason (R): Copyright protects the original expression of ideas in works.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false: ideas themselves are not protected. R is true, since copyright protects only the form in which an idea is expressed.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Companies Act, 2013, a company can own property and sue in its own name.
reason: Reason (R): Members of a company are personally liable for all the debts of the company.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true because a company is a separate legal person. R is false: in a company limited by shares, a member's liability is limited to the unpaid amount on his shares.

stem: The Goods and Services Tax was introduced in India through which constitutional amendment, enacted in 2016?
explanation: GST was enabled by the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016; '122nd' was the number of the Constitution Amendment Bill, not of the Act.

stem: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, arrange the following forums in the order in which a consumer dispute moves in appeal, starting from the original forum:
items: Supreme Court of India
National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
explanation: Appeals lie from the District Commission to the State Commission, from there to the National Commission and finally to the Supreme Court.

stem: Under the Competition Act, 2002, an agreement between competing enterprises that directly or indirectly fixes purchase or sale prices is:
options: Permitted if the parties are small enterprises
Examined only under the rule of reason
Presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition
explanation: Horizontal agreements such as price-fixing, output limitation, market sharing and bid rigging are presumed to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition (Section 3(3)).

stem: Consider the following statements about the structure of GST in India:
items: CGST and SGST are levied concurrently on intra-State supplies.
IGST is levied on inter-State supplies.
The GST Council is chaired by the Prime Minister.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The GST Council under Article 279A is chaired by the Union Finance Minister.

stem: Match List I (subject under the Competition Act, 2002) with List II (section):
listII: Section 4
Section 5
Section 6
Section 3
explanation: Section 3 prohibits anti-competitive agreements, Section 4 prohibits abuse of dominance, Section 5 defines combinations and Section 6 regulates them.

stem: The doctrine of 'caveat emptor' under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 means:
options: No one can give a better title than he himself has
Goods remain at the seller's risk until delivery
explanation: Caveat emptor means the buyer must satisfy himself about the goods; 'no one can give a better title than he has' is the separate nemo dat rule.

stem: Under the Companies Act, 2013, the maximum number of members of a private company (excluding certain present and former employee-members) is:
explanation: A private company's articles must limit its members to 200, excluding employees and ex-employees who became members during employment (the earlier 1956 Act limit was 50).

stem: Arrange the following special contracts in the order in which they are defined in the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
items: Pledge
Bailment
Guarantee
Agency (definition of agent)
Indemnity
explanation: Indemnity is defined in Section 124, guarantee in Section 126, bailment in Section 148, pledge in Section 172 and agent in Section 182.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, current account transactions are generally permitted, subject to reasonable restrictions notified by the Central Government.
reason: Reason (R): Under the Act, capital account transactions are regulated by the Reserve Bank of India in consultation with the Central Government.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both are true, but the regulation of capital account transactions does not explain why current account transactions are freely permitted; they are separate provisions.

stem: Match List I (factor affecting free consent under the Indian Contract Act, 1872) with List II (description):
listII: An innocent false statement which the maker believes to be true
A false representation made knowingly with intent to deceive
Committing or threatening an act forbidden by the penal law to obtain consent
Using a position to dominate another's will to obtain an unfair advantage
explanation: Coercion involves unlawful threats, undue influence abuses a dominating position, fraud requires intent to deceive, and misrepresentation is a false statement made without intent to deceive.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a cheque is always payable on demand.
reason: Reason (R): Under the Act, a cheque may be drawn on any person, not necessarily a banker.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true by definition of a cheque. R is false: a cheque must always be drawn on a specified banker.

stem: The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 replaced the:
explanation: FEMA, 1999 repealed and replaced FERA, 1973, which had itself replaced the earlier FERA of 1947.

stem: Arrange the following developments in India's foreign exchange regime in chronological order:
items: Enactment of the first Foreign Exchange Regulation Act
Enactment of the Foreign Exchange Management Act
Introduction of the Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS)
Re-enactment of FERA as a more stringent law
explanation: FERA was first enacted in 1947 and re-enacted in 1973; LERMS was introduced in 1992; FEMA was enacted in 1999.

stem: Match List I (implied term under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930) with List II (meaning):
listII: The bulk must correspond with the sample in quality
The goods must correspond with the description
The buyer shall have and enjoy undisturbed possession of the goods
The seller has a right to sell the goods
explanation: These are the standard implied conditions (title, description, sample) and the implied warranty of quiet possession.

stem: The Information Technology Act, 2000 is based on the:
options: UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce
explanation: The IT Act, 2000 was enacted in line with the UN General Assembly's adoption of the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce (1996) to give legal recognition to electronic transactions.

stem: According to the Privy Council in Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose, an agreement with a minor under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 is:
options: Valid if it is for the minor's benefit
Voidable at the option of the minor
Voidable at the option of the other party
explanation: Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903) held that a minor is not competent to contract, so an agreement with a minor is void from the beginning.

stem: Under the Patents Act, 1970 (as amended), the term of a patent is:
options: 60 years from the date of publication
10 years from the date of grant
14 years from the date of filing of the application
20 years from the date of filing of the application
explanation: After the 2002 amendment aligning with TRIPS, every patent has a term of 20 years from the date of filing, subject to payment of renewal fees.

stem: Match List I (party under the Indian Contract Act, 1872) with List II (description):
listII: Person who is promised protection against loss
Person who gives the guarantee
Person to whom goods are delivered as security for a debt
Person to whom goods are delivered for a purpose, to be returned or disposed of
explanation: The indemnity-holder is protected against loss, the surety gives the guarantee, the bailee receives goods under bailment, and the pawnee receives goods as security under a pledge.

stem: Consider the following statements with reference to the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008:
items: Every LLP must have at least two designated partners who are individuals, at least one of whom is resident in India.
The liability of every partner of an LLP is unlimited, as in a general partnership.
The LLP agreement governs the mutual rights and duties of the partners.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. An LLP is a separate legal entity and the liability of its partners is limited.

stem: Consider the following statements with reference to the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881:
items: A promissory note contains an unconditional order to pay.
A bill of exchange contains an unconditional order directing a certain person to pay.
A cheque is always drawn on a specified banker.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. A promissory note contains an unconditional undertaking (promise) to pay, whereas a bill of exchange contains an order.

stem: Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, arrange the following steps in a cheque-dishonour case in the correct order:
items: The payee files a complaint before the Magistrate within one month
The payee sends a written notice demanding payment within 30 days of receiving information of dishonour
The drawer fails to pay within 15 days of receiving the notice
The cheque is presented to the bank within its period of validity
The bank returns the cheque unpaid for insufficiency of funds
explanation: An offence under Section 138 arises only after presentation, dishonour, a demand notice within 30 days and failure to pay within 15 days of the notice; the complaint must then be filed within one month of the cause of action.

stem: Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agreement which is enforceable by law at the option of one or more of the parties, but not at the option of the other or others, is a:
explanation: Section 2(i) defines a voidable contract as one enforceable at the option of one or more parties but not of the other(s), e.g. a contract induced by coercion or fraud.

stem: Consider the following statements with reference to the Information Technology Act, 2000:
items: The Act applies to wills and other testamentary dispositions.
The Controller of Certifying Authorities licenses and regulates Certifying Authorities.
The 2008 amendment introduced the broader concept of electronic signatures in addition to digital signatures.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Wills and testamentary dispositions are among the documents to which the Act does not apply.

stem: Consider the following statements with reference to the definition of 'goods' under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930:
items: Stocks and shares are goods.
Money and actionable claims are goods.
Growing crops that are agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale are goods.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. 'Goods' means every kind of movable property other than actionable claims and money.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, an LLP is a body corporate having perpetual succession.
reason: Reason (R): Any change in the partners of an LLP does not affect its existence, rights or liabilities.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Perpetual succession means the LLP's existence continues irrespective of changes in its partners; R states exactly this, so R explains A.

stem: Under the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, the minimum number of partners required to form an LLP is:
explanation: Every LLP must have at least two partners; if the number falls below two for more than six months, the remaining partner may become personally liable.

stem: Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a contract to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person in case of his default is a contract of:
explanation: Section 126 defines a contract of guarantee; a contract of indemnity (Section 124) is a promise to save another from loss.

stem: Match List I (form of intellectual property) with List II (subject matter protected):
listII: A new invention involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application
Goods whose quality or reputation is attributable to their place of origin
Original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works
A mark capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from another
explanation: Patents protect inventions, copyright protects original works, trade marks protect distinguishing marks and geographical indications (e.g. Darjeeling tea) protect origin-linked goods.

stem: Consider the following statements about GST in India:
items: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is outside the scope of GST.
Petroleum crude is currently subject to GST at the standard rate.
Input tax credit allows tax paid on inputs to be set off against output tax liability.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. GST on petroleum crude, diesel, petrol, natural gas and ATF will apply only from a date recommended by the GST Council; till then they remain outside GST levy.

stem: Arrange the following events relating to indirect tax reform in India in chronological order:
items: Rollout of GST across the country
Enactment of the constitutional amendment enabling GST
Constitution of the GST Council
Introduction of state-level VAT in most States
explanation: Most States adopted VAT in 2005; the 101st Amendment was enacted in September 2016, the GST Council was constituted soon after in September 2016, and GST was rolled out on 1 July 2017.

stem: Assertion (A): GST in India is a destination-based consumption tax.
reason: Reason (R): Under GST, the tax revenue accrues to the State in which the goods or services are consumed.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The destination principle means tax follows consumption, so revenue goes to the consuming State; R explains why GST is called destination-based.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a contract of indemnity involves three parties: the creditor, the principal debtor and the surety.
reason: Reason (R): In a contract of indemnity, one party promises to save the other from loss caused by the conduct of the promisor himself or of any other person.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false: indemnity has two parties (indemnifier and indemnity-holder); three parties are found in a guarantee. R correctly paraphrases Section 124.

stem: Arrange the following steps in the incorporation of a company under the Companies Act, 2013 in the correct order:
items: Issue of the certificate of incorporation by the Registrar
Filing the declaration for commencement of business
Reserving the proposed name with the Registrar
Filing the incorporation documents along with the Memorandum and Articles
explanation: The name is reserved, incorporation documents with MoA and AoA are filed, the Registrar issues the certificate of incorporation, and the declaration for commencement of business is filed afterwards.

stem: Match List I (component of GST) with List II (levy):
listII: Levied by the Centre on inter-State supplies and imports
Levied by the Centre on intra-State supplies
Levied on intra-UT supplies in Union Territories without a legislature
Levied by a State on intra-State supplies
explanation: CGST and SGST are the Centre's and State's shares on intra-State supplies, IGST applies to inter-State supplies and imports, and UTGST replaces SGST in Union Territories without a legislature.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a promise to compensate a person who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor is enforceable even without fresh consideration.
reason: Reason (R): Compensation for past voluntary service is one of the statutory exceptions to the rule that an agreement without consideration is void.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Section 25 makes agreements without consideration void but excepts a promise to compensate for something voluntarily done for the promisor; that exception is exactly why A holds, so R explains A.

stem: Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, where the transfer of property in goods is to take place at a future time or subject to a condition to be fulfilled later, the contract is called:
explanation: In a sale, property passes immediately; where it is to pass in future or on fulfilment of a condition, it is an agreement to sell, which becomes a sale when the time elapses or the condition is met.

stem: Under the law of contract, a shopkeeper's display of priced goods in the shop window is:
options: A binding offer which the customer accepts by entering the shop
An invitation to treat (invitation to offer), not an offer
A standing offer that cannot be withdrawn
An acceptance of the customer's future offer
explanation: Display of priced goods merely invites customers to make offers; the contract is concluded when the shopkeeper accepts the customer's offer at the counter.

stem: Under Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a promise to pay a debt that is barred by limitation is enforceable if it is:
options: Supported by fresh consideration of equal value
Registered with the Registrar of Assurances
Made in writing and signed by the debtor or his authorised agent
explanation: Section 25(3) makes a written and signed promise to pay a time-barred debt enforceable without fresh consideration; an oral promise does not qualify.

stem: A agrees to sell to B a specific cargo of goods supposed to be on its way from England to Bombay. Unknown to both parties, the ship carrying the cargo had been wrecked and the goods lost before the agreement. Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the agreement is:
options: Voidable at the option of B
Valid, and A must pay damages to B
Void, because both parties were under a mistake as to a fact essential to the agreement
Valid, but unenforceable until the goods are replaced
explanation: Section 20: where both parties are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement, the agreement is void. The existence of the subject-matter is such a fact.

stem: According to the doctrine of privity of contract, as followed in India, a person who is not a party to a contract:
options: Can sue on it whenever it was made for his benefit
Can sue on it if he is a close relative of a party
Can sue on it only if he is a major
Cannot, as a general rule, sue on it even if it was made for his benefit
explanation: Only parties to a contract can enforce it; a stranger to the contract cannot sue on it except in recognised exceptions such as trusts, family settlements and assignments.

stem: A contractor completes half of the agreed work, after which the other party wrongfully prevents him from completing it. The contractor can claim reasonable remuneration for the work done under the principle of:
explanation: Quantum meruit means 'as much as he has earned': a party who has partly performed can claim a reasonable sum for work done where the other party prevents or repudiates the contract.

stem: Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, A contracts to pay B Rs 10,000 if B's house is burnt down. This contract is:
explanation: A contract to do or not to do something if some event collateral to the contract does or does not happen is a contingent contract (Section 31).

stem: Under the Indian Majority Act, 1875, a person domiciled in India, for whom no guardian has been appointed by a court, attains the age of majority on completing:
explanation: Majority is attained at 18 years (21 years where a court-appointed guardian exists or the property is under a court of wards). Capacity to contract under Section 11 of the Contract Act depends on this.

stem: Under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, where a sum is named in a contract as the amount payable on its breach, the party complaining of the breach is entitled to receive:
options: The entire named amount in every case
Only the actual loss proved, ignoring the named sum
Reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named
explanation: Section 74 allows reasonable compensation up to the stipulated amount, whether or not actual damage is proved; courts do not enforce penalties as such.

stem: Under Section 62 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, when the parties to a contract agree to substitute a new contract for the existing one, the original contract need not be performed. This is called:
explanation: Novation is the substitution of a new contract for the old by mutual agreement, which discharges the original contract.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a person who has attained majority cannot ratify an agreement made by him during minority.
reason: Reason (R): An agreement with a minor is void ab initio and therefore cannot be validated by subsequent ratification.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Since the minor's agreement is void from the beginning, nothing exists to be ratified, and consideration for the ratifying promise would be past consideration. R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): Under Section 7 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, acceptance of a proposal must be absolute and unqualified.
reason: Reason (R): A counter-proposal made by the offeree keeps the original proposal alive so that it can still be accepted later.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true. R is false: a counter-proposal operates as a rejection of the original proposal, which then lapses.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agreement caused by a mistake of both parties as to a law in force in India is void.
reason: Reason (R): Under the Act, a mistake as to a law not in force in India has the same effect as a mistake of fact.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Section 21: a contract is not voidable merely because it was caused by a mistake as to any law in force in India, so A is false. R correctly states the second part of Section 21.

stem: Assertion (A): A contract of fire insurance is not a wagering agreement.
reason: Reason (R): A contract of insurance is a contract of utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei).
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true because the insured has an insurable interest, which a wager lacks. R is also true but is a separate feature of insurance and does not explain why it is not a wager.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a proposer may revoke his proposal at any time before the communication of acceptance is complete as against him, but not afterwards.
reason: Reason (R): As against the proposer, the communication of acceptance is complete when it is put in the course of transmission to him so as to be out of the power of the acceptor to withdraw it.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Section 5 fixes the last moment of revocation by reference to when acceptance is complete as against the proposer, which is exactly what R states.

stem: Assertion (A): Under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a contract becomes void when its performance becomes impossible or unlawful after the contract is made.
reason: Reason (R): 'Impossible' in Section 56 covers only literal physical impossibility and never the frustration of the object of the contract.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true (supervening impossibility). R is false: the Supreme Court in Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur held 'impossible' includes practical impossibility, where the object of the contract is frustrated.

stem: Consider the following statements about consideration under the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
items: Consideration may be past, present or future.
An agreement is void if the consideration is not adequate in value.
A promise to do what the promisor is already legally bound to do is not good consideration.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: The Act's definition covers acts done or abstained from 'has done or abstained from doing, does or abstains, or promises' (past, present, future). Inadequacy does not by itself invalidate an agreement. Doing what one is already bound to do confers nothing new.

stem: Consider the following statements about void agreements under the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
items: An agreement to refer future disputes to arbitration is void as a restraint of legal proceedings.
An agreement whose meaning is not certain, or capable of being made certain, is void.
An agreement which absolutely restricts a party from enforcing his rights by the usual legal proceedings is void to that extent.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Section 29 makes uncertain agreements void; Section 28 voids agreements restraining legal proceedings or limiting the time for enforcement. Statement 1 is wrong because Section 28 expressly saves arbitration agreements.

stem: Consider the following statements about discharge of contract under the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
items: A promisee may extend the time for performance or accept a lesser satisfaction in place of full performance.
A contract based on the personal skill of the promisor is discharged by his death.
A valid tender of performance refused by the promisee deprives the promisor of his rights under the contract.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Section 63 allows remission, extension of time or acceptance of lesser satisfaction; a personal-service contract ends with the promisor's death. Under Section 38 a refused valid tender does not make the promisor lose his rights.

stem: Consider the following statements about compensation for breach under Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
items: Compensation is payable for loss which naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach.
Compensation is payable for any remote and indirect loss resulting from the breach.
Compensation is payable for loss which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Section 73 allows damages for natural loss and for loss within the parties' contemplation at the time of contracting, but not for remote or indirect loss.

stem: Consider the following statements about minors under the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
items: The property of a minor is liable to reimburse a person who supplied him with necessaries suited to his condition in life.
A minor may be a promisee and can enforce a promise made in his favour if he has no obligation left to perform.
A minor who obtained a contract by falsely representing himself to be a major is estopped from pleading minority.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Section 68 reimburses suppliers of necessaries out of the minor's property (not by personal liability). A minor can be a beneficiary or promisee. In India no estoppel operates against a minor (Mohori Bibee), though restitution of benefits may be ordered under equity.

stem: Consider the following statements about quasi-contracts under the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
items: A person who lawfully does something for another, not intended to be gratuitous, and the other enjoys the benefit, must be compensated.
A person to whom money has been paid by mistake or under coercion must repay it.
The obligation in a quasi-contract is imposed by law and does not arise from any agreement between the parties.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Sections 70 and 72 respectively cover statements 1 and 2; quasi-contractual obligations are created by law on grounds of equity and justice, not by agreement.

stem: Match List I (section of the Indian Contract Act, 1872) with List II (subject):
listII: Agreement to do an impossible act; supervening impossibility
What considerations and objects are lawful and what not
What agreements are contracts
Agreement without consideration is void, unless it falls under stated exceptions
explanation: Section 10 states the essentials of a contract, Section 23 lawful consideration and object, Section 25 the rule on agreements without consideration and its exceptions, and Section 56 impossibility.

stem: Match List I (type of contract) with List II (description):
listII: Rights and obligations arise from the conduct of the parties or the circumstances of the case
Terms are stated in words, oral or written
Obligation imposed by law without any agreement
Performance is still to be made, wholly or partly, by one or both parties
explanation: Express contracts are in words; implied contracts arise from conduct; executory contracts are yet to be performed; quasi-contracts are imposed by law.

stem: Match List I (case) with List II (principle established):
listI: Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.
listII: A general offer can be accepted by performing its conditions
Damages are limited to loss that was not too remote
Acceptance of an offer requires knowledge of the offer
Domestic arrangements lack intention to create legal relations
explanation: Carlill: general offer by performance; Hadley: remoteness of damages; Lalman Shukla: acceptance without knowledge of the offer is no acceptance; Balfour: domestic agreements are not contracts.

stem: Match List I (provision of Section 2 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872) with List II (what it defines):
listII: Consideration: something done or abstained from at the desire of the promisor
Agreement: every promise and every set of promises forming consideration for each other
An agreement not enforceable by law
An agreement enforceable by law
explanation: Section 2(d) consideration, 2(e) agreement, 2(g) void agreement, 2(h) contract.

stem: Arrange the following stages in the formation and life of a contract under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 in the correct order:
items: Acceptance of the proposal
Making of a proposal
Discharge of the contract by performance
The agreement becomes enforceable at law as a contract
explanation: A proposal is made, accepted to form an agreement, which becomes a contract when enforceable by law, and is finally discharged on performance.

stem: Arrange the following subjects in the order in which they appear in the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
items: Free consent
Contingent contracts
Compensation for breach of contract
Capacity of parties to contract
explanation: Capacity (Section 11), free consent (Sections 13-22), contingent contracts (Section 31) and compensation for breach (Section 73) appear in that sequence.

stem: Arrange the following events in a case of anticipatory breach of contract in the correct order:
items: The promisor repudiates performance before the due date
The aggrieved party claims damages for the breach
The contract is made, with performance due on a future date
The aggrieved party elects to treat the contract as discharged
explanation: After the contract is made, repudiation before the due date gives the promisee the option to treat the contract as ended and then sue for damages.

stem: Under Section 125 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the promisee in a contract of indemnity, acting within the scope of his authority, can recover from the promisor:
options: Only the principal amount of damages, excluding costs of the suit
All damages he is compelled to pay in a suit on the matter covered by the indemnity, the costs of the suit, and sums paid under a bona fide compromise
Only sums paid after a final decree of a court
Nothing, until the promisor himself has been sued by the third party
explanation: Section 125 gives the indemnity-holder damages, costs (if he acted prudently or on the promisor's orders) and compromise sums, which is wider than the other options.

stem: Under Section 127 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in a contract of guarantee, anything done or any promise made for the benefit of the principal debtor:
options: Is not consideration, because the surety receives nothing himself
Is consideration only if the surety is also paid a commission
May be a sufficient consideration to the surety for giving the guarantee
Is consideration only if it is made before the guarantee is given
explanation: Section 127 provides that the benefit conferred on the principal debtor is sufficient consideration for the surety's promise; the surety need not benefit personally.

stem: Under Section 131 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, the death of the surety in a continuing guarantee operates as a revocation:
options: As regards all transactions, past as well as future
Not at all, since the legal heirs remain bound for future transactions
Only if the principal debtor consents to it
explanation: Death of the surety revokes a continuing guarantee only for future transactions; his estate stays liable for liabilities already incurred.

stem: A stands surety for B's repayment of a loan taken from C. Without A's consent, C and B vary the terms of the loan agreement. Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, A is:
options: Not discharged, since the creditor may still proceed against the surety
Discharged as to all transactions, including those before the variance
Discharged only if he gives notice of the variance to C
Discharged as to transactions subsequent to the variance
explanation: Section 133: any variance made without the surety's consent in the terms of the contract between principal debtor and creditor discharges the surety as to subsequent transactions.

stem: Under Section 151 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in all cases of bailment the bailee must take as much care of the goods bailed as:
options: A man of ordinary prudence would, in similar circumstances, take of his own goods of the same bulk, quality and value
He takes of his own goods, whatever their value
An expert dealing in such goods would take
A trustee of a public charity would take
explanation: The standard is objective (ordinary prudence), applied to goods of the same bulk, quality and value as those bailed.

stem: Under Section 71 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a person who finds goods belonging to another and takes them into his custody is subject to the same responsibility as:
explanation: Section 71 places the finder of goods under the responsibility of a bailee, including the duty of reasonable care and of not appropriating the goods.

stem: Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, if a pawnor defaults on the stipulated date but the pledged goods have not yet been sold, he may redeem the goods by paying:
options: Only the debt, without any additional expenses
Double the amount of the debt
The debt together with any expenses arising from his default
The market value of the goods
explanation: Section 177 allows the pawnor to redeem at any time before actual sale, on paying the debt and any expenses arising from his default.

stem: Under Section 189 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in an emergency an agent has authority to:
options: Do nothing until he obtains fresh instructions from the principal
Do any act, even if it exceeds what a prudent person would do
Appoint a sub-agent and transfer all liability to him
Do all such acts for protecting his principal from loss as would be done by a person of ordinary prudence in his own case
explanation: Authority in an emergency is implied by law and measured by the conduct of an ordinarily prudent person acting to protect his own interests.

stem: A person by words or conduct leads a third party to believe that another is his agent, although he has given no authority. Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the first person is bound to the third party who acted on that belief under the principle of:
explanation: Section 237 binds a principal who has by his conduct induced a third party to believe the acts were authorised; this is agency by estoppel.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a person who is not the owner of goods cannot, as a general rule, make a valid pledge of them.
reason: Reason (R): No one can give a better title to goods than he himself has (nemo dat quod non habet).
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The general rule against pledges by non-owners rests on nemo dat; Sections 178 and 178A are the statutory exceptions. R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): In a contract of bailment under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, ownership of the goods passes to the bailee.
reason: Reason (R): After the purpose of bailment is accomplished, the goods must be returned or disposed of according to the bailor's directions.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false: only possession is transferred in bailment, ownership stays with the bailor. R is true (Section 148) and is the reason ownership cannot have passed.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agent who makes a secret profit in the course of the agency must account for it to his principal.
reason: Reason (R): An agent stands in a fiduciary relationship with the principal.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The agent's duty to account arises from the fiduciary character of the relationship, which forbids profit at the principal's expense without disclosure.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a guarantee obtained by the creditor's concealment of a material circumstance is invalid.
reason: Reason (R): A guarantee obtained by means of misrepresentation made by the creditor, or with his knowledge and assent, is also invalid.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Section 143 (concealment) and Section 142 (misrepresentation) are separate grounds of invalidity; both are true but R does not explain A.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a bailor must disclose to the bailee faults in the goods which he knows of and which materially interfere with their use or expose the bailee to extraordinary risks.
reason: Reason (R): Where the goods are bailed for hire, the bailor is not responsible for damage resulting from faults in the goods, even if he knew of them.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true (Section 150). R is false: in a bailment for hire the bailor is responsible for damage from faults whether or not he knew of them.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a principal may always terminate the agency at any time, even if the agent has an interest in the subject-matter of the agency.
reason: Reason (R): Where the agent has himself an interest in the property which forms the subject-matter of the agency, the agency cannot, in the absence of an express contract, be terminated to the prejudice of that interest.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Section 202 protects an agency coupled with interest, so A is false. R accurately states Section 202.

stem: Consider the following statements about the discharge of a surety under the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
items: A continuing guarantee may at any time be revoked by the surety, as to future transactions, by notice to the creditor.
Mere forbearance by the creditor to sue the principal debtor discharges the surety.
A contract between the creditor and the principal debtor by which the principal debtor is released discharges the surety.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Sections 130 and 134 make statements 1 and 3 correct. Under Section 137, mere forbearance to sue the principal debtor does not discharge the surety unless the contract provides so.

stem: Consider the following statements about the rights of a surety under the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
items: A surety who has paid the debt is invested with all the rights the creditor had against the principal debtor.
The principal debtor is under an implied promise to indemnify the surety.
Co-sureties are liable to contribute in proportion to their financial means, in the absence of a contract to the contrary.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Sections 140 (subrogation) and 145 (implied indemnity) are correct. Under Section 146 co-sureties contribute equally, not in proportion to means.

stem: Consider the following statements about bailment under the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
items: The bailee must return the goods without demand once the time for bailment has expired or the purpose has been accomplished.
A gratuitous bailment is terminated by the death of either the bailor or the bailee.
A bailee who has rendered service in respect of the goods has a right to retain them until he is paid for that service, in the absence of a contract to the contrary.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Section 160 (return without demand), Section 162 (death ends gratuitous bailment) and Section 170 (particular lien) are all correct.

stem: Consider the following statements about pledge under the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
items: A pledge may be made of immovable property by delivering its possession to the pawnee.
The pawnee may retain the pledged goods for payment of the debt, interest on it and necessary expenses incurred for possession or preservation of the goods.
Unless a contract provides otherwise, the pawnee cannot retain the goods for a debt other than the one for which they were pledged.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Sections 173 and 174 support statements 2 and 3. Pledge is a bailment of goods only, so statement 1 is wrong.

stem: Consider the following statements about ratification of an agent's unauthorised act under the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
items: A person who ratifies an unauthorised act ratifies the whole of the transaction of which that act formed a part.
Ratification must be express and in writing to be valid.
No valid ratification can be made by a person whose knowledge of the facts of the case is only incomplete or whose consent is obtained without full knowledge.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Section 199 requires ratification of the whole transaction and Section 198 requires full knowledge of the facts. Section 197 allows ratification to be express or implied, so statement 2 is wrong.

stem: Consider the following statements about the personal liability of an agent under the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
items: In the absence of a contract to the contrary, an agent who contracts for a disclosed principal is presumed not to be personally bound by the contract.
An agent who makes a contract for the sale or purchase of goods for a merchant resident abroad is presumed, in the absence of a contrary contract, to be personally liable.
An agent for a disclosed principal can generally sue personally on contracts he makes for the principal.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Section 230 states the presumption in statements 1 and 2. It also says that such an agent cannot personally enforce contracts made for the principal, so statement 3 is wrong.

stem: Match List I (section of the Indian Contract Act, 1872) with List II (subject):
listII: Bailment of goods as security for a loan or promise
Contract of bailment
Contract of guarantee
Contract of indemnity
explanation: Section 124 defines indemnity, 126 guarantee, 148 bailment and 172 pledge.

stem: Match List I (type of agent) with List II (description):
listII: Negotiates contracts between buyer and seller without having possession of the goods
A person employed by and acting under the control of the original agent
Entrusted with possession of goods and authorised to sell them in his own name
For an extra commission, guarantees to the principal that buyers will pay
explanation: A del credere agent guarantees the buyer's payment; a factor has possession and sells in his own name; a broker only negotiates; a sub-agent works under the agent's control.

stem: Match List I (term in the law of guarantee) with List II (meaning):
listII: A guarantee limited to a single, specified debt or transaction
The surety, on paying, steps into the creditor's shoes against the principal debtor
A guarantee extending to a series of transactions
A person jointly liable with the surety for the same debt
explanation: A continuing guarantee covers a series of transactions; a specific guarantee a single one; co-sureties share liability; subrogation lets the surety use the creditor's rights.

stem: Match List I (section of the Indian Contract Act, 1872) with List II (provision):
listII: Termination of agency
Definition of 'agent' and 'principal'
Ratification of acts done without authority
No consideration necessary to create an agency
explanation: Section 182 defines agent and principal, 185 dispenses with consideration, 196 deals with ratification and 201 with termination of agency.

stem: Arrange the following steps in the enforcement of a pledge on the pawnor's default under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 in the correct order:
items: The pawnee gives the pawnor reasonable notice of the intended sale
The pawnor delivers the goods to the pawnee as security for a debt
The pawnee sells the goods after the notice period
The pawnor fails to pay the debt on the due date
explanation: Delivery creates the pledge, default allows enforcement, and under Section 176 the pawnee may sell only after giving reasonable notice.

stem: Arrange the following events in a guarantee transaction, ending with the surety's remedy against the principal debtor, in the correct order:
items: The surety pays the creditor
The creditor demands payment from the surety
The surety recovers the amount from the principal debtor
The principal debtor defaults on the loan
explanation: Default by the principal debtor leads to demand on the surety, who pays and then, by subrogation and the implied promise of indemnity, recovers from the principal debtor.

stem: Arrange the following stages of a bailment in the correct order:
items: The purpose of the bailment is accomplished or the stipulated time expires
The bailor delivers the goods to the bailee for a specified purpose
The bailee holds or uses the goods only for that purpose
The bailee returns the goods to the bailor
explanation: Delivery begins the bailment; the bailee holds the goods for the purpose; on completion or expiry he must return the goods.

stem: A exchanges 10 bags of wheat for 5 bags of rice with B. Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, this transaction is:
options: A contract of sale, since both parties transfer goods of value
Not a contract of sale, because the consideration is not a money price
An agreement to sell, since delivery is postponed
A contract of bailment of goods
explanation: A contract of sale requires a price, i.e. money consideration. An exchange of goods for goods is barter and falls outside the Act's definition of sale.

stem: Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, a contract is made for the sale of specific goods which, without the seller's knowledge, had already perished at the time the contract was made. The contract is:
options: Voidable at the option of the buyer
Valid, with the seller liable for damages
Valid, with the price payable by the buyer
explanation: Section 7: a contract for specific goods which, unknown to the seller, have perished at the time of contract is void.

stem: Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, breach of a warranty by the seller entitles the buyer to:
options: Reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated
Cancel the contract and recover the full price in all cases
No remedy, because a warranty is only collateral
Claim damages, but not to reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated
explanation: A warranty is collateral to the main purpose of the contract; its breach gives a right to damages only, unlike breach of a condition.

stem: Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, where a contract of sale is not severable and the buyer has accepted the goods, breach of a condition by the seller can, unless the contract provides otherwise, be treated only as:
options: A criminal offence against the buyer
explanation: Under Section 13, once the buyer has accepted the goods (in a non-severable contract), breach of condition is treated as breach of warranty and gives damages only.

stem: A tells a chemist that he needs a lotion for a particular skin allergy and relies on the chemist's skill in choosing it. The lotion aggravates his condition. Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, A can claim breach of:
options: The implied condition as to the seller's title to the goods
The implied condition that the goods are reasonably fit for the purpose made known to the seller
The implied warranty of quiet possession
The implied warranty that the goods are free from encumbrance
explanation: Section 16(1): where the buyer makes known the particular purpose and relies on the seller's skill or judgment, there is an implied condition of reasonable fitness for that purpose.

stem: Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, as a general rule, where goods are sold by a person who is not their owner and who has no authority to sell, a buyer acting in good faith acquires:
options: A good title in all cases
A good title if he has paid the full price
No better title than the seller had
A voidable title which the true owner may confirm
explanation: Section 27 states the nemo dat rule: no one can transfer a better title than he has, subject to the statutory exceptions (mercantile agents, voidable title, etc.).

stem: Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, where goods are shipped and the bill of lading makes the goods deliverable to the order of the seller or his agent, the seller is prima facie deemed to have:
options: Transferred the property in the goods to the buyer
Waived his right of lien over the goods
Reserved the right of disposal of the goods
Lost his right of stoppage in transit
explanation: Section 25(2): shipping on a bill of lading deliverable to the seller's order shows an intention to reserve the right of disposal, so property does not pass to the buyer.

stem: Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, unless otherwise agreed, goods remain at the seller's risk until:
options: The price is paid in full
The property in them is transferred to the buyer
explanation: Section 26 follows the maxim res perit domino: risk prima facie passes with the property, not with payment or possession.

stem: Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, where the property in goods has passed to the buyer and he wrongfully neglects or refuses to pay for them according to the contract, the seller may:
options: Sue the buyer for the price of the goods
Sue only for damages for non-acceptance, never for the price
Rescind the contract without any notice
Retain the goods and keep the money already received as a penalty
explanation: Section 55(1): once property has passed and the buyer wrongfully refuses to pay, the seller can sue for the price.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, an unpaid seller can exercise the right of stoppage in transit only when the buyer becomes insolvent.
reason: Reason (R): The right of stoppage in transit allows an unpaid seller who has parted with possession to resume possession of goods that are on their way to the buyer.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both statements are true (Section 50 and the nature of the right), but R only describes what the right is; it does not explain why insolvency is the condition.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, if the seller had no right to sell the goods, the buyer can ordinarily recover the full price paid even though he has used the goods for some time.
reason: Reason (R): The buyer's purpose in buying is to acquire ownership, so a failure of title is a total failure of consideration.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: This is the reasoning in Rowland v. Divall: the buyer got nothing of what he bargained for, so the price is recoverable in full. R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, in a sale by sample, the seller is not liable for a defect in the bulk that would not be apparent on a reasonable examination of the sample, provided the bulk matches the sample in quality.
reason: Reason (R): In a sale by sample, there is an implied condition that the buyer shall have a reasonable opportunity of comparing the bulk with the sample.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false: Section 17 also implies a condition that the goods are free from any defect rendering them unmerchantable which would not be apparent on reasonable examination of the sample. R is true.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, stipulations as to the time of payment are not deemed to be of the essence of a contract of sale unless a different intention appears from the contract.
reason: Reason (R): Under the Act, stipulations as to the time of delivery are always of the essence of the contract.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true (Section 11). R is false: whether any other stipulation as to time is of the essence depends on the terms of the contract.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, there is no implied condition of merchantable quality as regards defects which the buyer's examination of the goods ought to have revealed.
reason: Reason (R): A buyer who examines the goods before buying is presumed to rely on his own judgment and not on the seller's.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The proviso to the implied condition of merchantable quality excludes defects the buyer ought to have found on examination, reflecting the buyer's reliance on his own judgment.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, where goods are sold by sample as well as by description, it is not sufficient that the bulk corresponds with the sample if it does not correspond with the description.
reason: Reason (R): The implied conditions as to sample and as to description are independent, and both must be satisfied.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Section 15 makes correspondence with both sample and description a requirement; failing either breaches an implied condition. R explains A.

stem: Consider the following statements about conditions and warranties under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930:
items: Breach of a condition gives the buyer the right to treat the contract as repudiated.
Whether a stipulation is a condition or a warranty depends on the label the parties have given it.
A buyer may waive a condition or elect to treat its breach as a breach of warranty.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 and 3 follow Sections 12 and 13. Statement 2 is wrong: the nature of the stipulation depends on the construction of the contract, not on its label.

stem: Consider the following statements about price under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930:
items: The price may be fixed by the contract, left to be fixed in a manner agreed, or determined by the course of dealing between the parties.
Where the price is not determined in any of these ways, the buyer must pay a reasonable price.
A contract of sale in which the price is left to be fixed later is void for uncertainty.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Section 9 covers statements 1 and 2. A contract is not void merely because the price is to be fixed later in an agreed manner.

stem: Consider the following statements about the transfer of property in goods under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930:
items: In a contract for the sale of unascertained goods, the property passes to the buyer when the contract is made.
In an unconditional contract for specific goods in a deliverable state, the property passes when the contract is made, even if payment or delivery is postponed.
Where goods are delivered on approval, the property passes when the buyer signifies approval or, without giving notice of rejection, retains the goods beyond the fixed or a reasonable time.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 2 and 3 reflect Sections 20 and 24. Statement 1 is wrong because Section 18 says no property passes in unascertained goods until they are ascertained.

stem: Consider the following statements about acceptance and delivery under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930:
items: The buyer is deemed to have accepted the goods when, after a reasonable time, he retains them without intimating rejection to the seller.
If the seller delivers less than the contracted quantity, the buyer must accept it and pay at the contract rate.
A buyer who rightly refuses to accept delivery is not bound to return the goods to the seller.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Sections 42 and 43 support statements 1 and 3. Under Section 37 the buyer may reject a short delivery; if he accepts it he pays at the contract rate.

stem: Consider the following statements about sale by auction under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930:
items: Once a bid is made, the bidder cannot retract it before the auctioneer announces completion of the sale.
Where goods are put up for sale in lots, each lot is prima facie the subject of a separate contract of sale.
If the seller uses pretended bidding to raise the price, the sale is voidable at the option of the buyer.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Under Section 64 any bidder may retract his bid until the sale is announced complete, so statement 1 is wrong; statements 2 and 3 are correct.

stem: Consider the following exceptions to the rule that a non-owner cannot pass a good title under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930:
items: A joint owner in sole possession with the co-owners' permission sells to a buyer in good faith without notice of his lack of authority.
A person in possession of goods under a voidable contract sells them to a bona fide buyer before the contract is avoided.
A seller who continues in possession after the sale delivers the goods to another buyer who acts in good faith without notice of the previous sale.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Each is a statutory exception to the nemo dat rule, protecting a bona fide buyer.

stem: Match List I (section of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930) with List II (subject):
listII: Effect of non-ascertainment of goods on the passing of property
Sale by a person who is not the owner
Meaning of condition and warranty
Sale and agreement to sell
explanation: Section 4 defines sale and agreement to sell, Section 12 condition and warranty, Section 18 ascertainment of goods and Section 27 sale by a non-owner.

stem: Match List I (mode of delivery of goods) with List II (description):
listII: Delivery of a key or document of title that gives control over the goods
Physical transfer of the goods to the buyer
Delivery of part of the goods in the course of delivering the whole, which has the same effect as delivery of the whole
A person holding the goods acknowledges that he holds them on behalf of the buyer
explanation: Actual delivery is physical; constructive delivery is by attornment; symbolic delivery is by a key or document; part delivery in progress of the whole counts as delivery of the whole.

stem: Match List I (kind of goods) with List II (meaning):
listII: Goods owned or possessed by the seller at the time of the contract
Goods to be manufactured, produced or acquired by the seller after making the contract
Goods identified and agreed upon at the time the contract is made
Goods defined only by description or genus and not yet identified
explanation: Specific goods are identified at the time of contract; future goods do not yet belong to the seller; existing goods are owned or possessed by him; unascertained goods are identified only by description.

stem: Match List I (remedy of an unpaid seller) with List II (nature of the remedy):
listII: Sell the goods, after notice where required, to recover the price
Retain possession of the goods until the price is paid or tendered
Sue the buyer personally where property has passed and he wrongfully refuses to pay
Resume possession of goods in transit when the buyer becomes insolvent
explanation: Lien is retention of possession; resale is a right against the goods; stoppage in transit requires the buyer's insolvency; a suit for the price is a personal remedy against the buyer.

stem: Arrange the following steps in a sale by auction in the correct order:
items: The auctioneer announces completion of the sale by the fall of the hammer
Bidders make successively higher bids
The goods are put up for sale in lots
The buyer takes delivery of the goods on payment
explanation: Goods are put up, bids are made, the sale is completed by the fall of the hammer, and delivery follows on payment.

stem: Arrange the following steps in the exercise of an unpaid seller's right of resale under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 in the correct order:
items: The buyer fails to pay within a reasonable time after the notice
The unpaid seller retains possession of the goods under his lien
The seller gives notice to the buyer of his intention to resell
The seller resells the goods and claims any loss from the original buyer
explanation: The seller holds the goods, gives notice of resale, the buyer defaults after a reasonable time, and only then does the seller resell and claim the shortfall.

stem: Arrange the following steps in the passing of property in unascertained goods under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 in the correct order:
items: The goods are unconditionally appropriated to the contract with the assent of the other party
A contract is made for the sale of unascertained goods
The property in the goods passes to the buyer
Goods answering the contract description are identified
explanation: After the contract, the goods must be ascertained (Section 18) and unconditionally appropriated with assent (Section 23); only then does property pass.

stem: Arrange the following subjects in the order in which they appear in the Sale of Goods Act, 1930:
items: Suits for breach of the contract
Effects of the contract (transfer of property)
Conditions and warranties
Rights of the unpaid seller against the goods
explanation: The Act deals with conditions and warranties, then effects of the contract, then performance and the unpaid seller's rights, and finally suits for breach.

stem: The three original parties to a bill of exchange under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, are:
explanation: A bill of exchange is an order by the drawer directing the drawee to pay the payee. A promissory note, by contrast, has a maker and a payee only.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a condition for a person to be a holder in due course under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881?
options: He took the instrument for consideration
He became its possessor before the amount became payable
He had no sufficient cause to believe that the transferor's title was defective
He received the instrument directly from the drawer or maker
explanation: A holder in due course may take the instrument from any prior holder; direct receipt from the drawer or maker is not required. The other three are the conditions of consideration, taking before maturity and good faith.

stem: Under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a cheque payable to bearer can be negotiated by:
options: Endorsement and delivery, both being compulsory
explanation: A bearer instrument is negotiated by mere delivery; endorsement and delivery are needed only for an instrument payable to order.

stem: Rajiv, in Delhi, draws a bill of exchange on a merchant resident in Dubai, payable at Dubai. Under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, this bill is:
explanation: An instrument drawn in India is inland only if it is payable in India or drawn on a person resident in India. This bill is neither, so it is a foreign bill.

stem: An endorser writes 'sans recourse' above his signature while endorsing a bill of exchange. The effect is that he:
options: Transfers no title to the endorsee
Excludes his own liability to later holders if the bill is dishonoured
Becomes the principal debtor on the bill
explanation: By express words an endorser may exclude his own liability on the instrument. The bill remains negotiable and the endorsee still gets title.

stem: A banker pays a cheque according to its apparent tenor, in good faith and without negligence, to the person in possession of it, in circumstances that give no reasonable ground to doubt that person's right to receive payment. This is known as:
explanation: The Act calls such a payment 'payment in due course', and it discharges the instrument and protects the paying banker.

stem: Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, dishonour of a cheque issued in discharge of a debt becomes an offence when the cheque is returned unpaid because:
options: The drawee bank's computer system was not working
The payee died before presenting it
